title: AP Exclusive: ICE Quietly Removes Thousands of Detainees with Final Removal Orders from Public Locator
detail: The Associated Press reported September 21, 2026 that ICE stopped publicly listing the locations of thousands of detainees with final orders of removal, an unannounced change made to its online detainee locator system on September 15, 2026. The change makes it far harder for lawyers and family members to find where a detainee is being held. Roughly 30% of ICE's 65,000+ detainees as of July 2026 had final removal orders, and nearly 16,000 people booked into ICE detention in July alone were subject to final removal orders — more than a third of that month's bookings. Immigration lawyers told AP that clients 'disappeared' from the system without warning; the American Immigration Lawyers Association (AILA) warned members on Friday, September 18, with one organization saying 'every single one of our clients who has a final order has disappeared from the locator,' documenting 17 such cases by Monday, September 21. Lawyers said the change could make last-minute legal challenges to removal 'nearly impossible.' ICE did not confirm or deny the change but said detainees with final removal orders are being prioritized for deportation amid 'a historic number of injunctions' blocking individual removals. The exclusion does not apply to detainees at Adelanto, California or temporary holding facilities in Minneapolis, New York City, or suburban Chicago, where courts have ordered ICE to list new arrivals promptly.

title: DHS Awards Up to $7.3 Billion in Construction Contracts to Expand ICE Detention in Five States
detail: DHS signed five Indefinite Delivery, Indefinite Quantity (IDIQ) construction contracts worth up to $7.3 billion on Sunday, September 21, 2026, to expand ICE detention capacity on government-owned land in New York (Batavia, expanding the existing ICE detention center — $1.5B to Rapid Deployment Inc. of Alabama), Texas (El Paso, new capacity on government property — $2.2B to Rapid Deployment Inc.), Arizona (Florence, expanding the existing ICE detention center — $1.2B to GardaWorld Federal Services), Florida (Miami, new capacity at an unspecified site — $1.2B to GardaWorld Federal Services), and California (El Centro, a former ICE facility now used by the U.S. Marshals Service, which has not held ICE detainees since 2014 — $1.2B to Rudiarius Holdings Corp.). DHS separately announced it will also expand detention in Colorado, Washington, and Pennsylvania. The contracts are part of a roughly $10 billion detention-construction program funded by the $75 billion immigration-enforcement supplement in the 'One Big Beautiful Bill Act'; standardized secure-housing units of 26 steel cells are estimated to cost $24–42 million each, though DHS has not disclosed total bed counts or construction schedules, and no construction has begun pending task orders and further appropriations. GEO Group CEO George Zoley said the company currently manages 68,000 ICE detention beds nationwide and that ICE is aiming for roughly 100,000 operational beds.
